description: A small software engineering team specializing in secure systems, data-driven applications, and mission-critical software. The focus is on transforming complex NASA data into a reliable, intuitive, and technically rigorous lunar mission-planning tool designed for clarity, efficiency, and real-world usability.
summary:
At the Moon's south pole the Sun and the Earth never climb more than a few degrees above the horizon, so a single ridge decides whether a lander has power and a radio link. Choosing a landing site means asking, place after place and date after date: if we land here, on this day, will we have power, and can we talk to Earth?

Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers it in seconds. It places the Sun and the Earth against the real skyline of each site, computed from NASA's LOLA elevation model, and compares up to four sites and landing dates side by side: sunlight, longest night, windows of contact with the Earth, longest link gap, eclipses included. A live map shows where sunlight and the Earth are in view at any moment; a calendar shows what every landing day of the coming year would give; and for a mission described in a few words it ranks the best sites and landing dates.

It runs entirely in the browser, on public NASA data, and its results are checked against NASA's own: JPL Horizons, the LOLA illumination maps, NASA's eclipse predictions and real landings.

Try it: https://m4tt187.github.io/lunar-landing-site-navigator/
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Landing Site Navigator compares up to four scenarios side by side. A scenario is a site, a landing date and the height of the solar panels or antenna above the ground. A table marks the better value for sunlight, longest night, Earth visibility, longest link gap, and power and link together.

For each scenario it shows the sky the lander would see: the real skyline all around the site, the paths of the Sun and the Earth over the mission, true-scale close-ups of the solar disc and of the Earth against the ridge line, and the time left to the next sunset, sunrise, Earthset or Earthrise. One slider, or Play, moves every scenario through its mission.

A map answers "where?". For everything south of 80° S it shows where the Sun and the Earth are in view at this moment, with shadows that move as time plays, and the share of the mission with sunlight, with the Earth in view, and with both. It names the best place for power and link within 5 km of the selected site. The map can be zoomed and dragged.

A calendar answers "when?". For every landing day of the coming year it shows how long sunlight, the Earth link, or both would last unbroken after touchdown, with the best landing days marked.

A recommendation answers "which?". Describe the mission (so many days of operations, a lander that survives so many hours of darkness, the Earth in view at touchdown or not) and it searches every site with a real skyline and every landing hour of a year, and ranks the best site-and-date pairs: power for the whole mission first, then the most contact with the Earth. One click puts an answer into the comparison.

Sites to start from: Apollo and robotic landing sites with cited coordinates, named south-pole features, the eight best-lit points of NASA's long-term illumination map, or any point typed or clicked on the map. Eclipses of the Sun by the Earth are included, in the numbers and on the map. The rules can be changed: what counts as "Sun up" (any part of the disc, half, or all of it) and as "Earth in view" (its centre on the skyline, or 2° or 5° above it). A link reproduces any comparison exactly. Plain-language sentences accompany the numbers, so the same screen serves a planner who wants degrees and hours and a student who wants to know why the pole is hard.

HOW IT WORKS

Everything is computed in the browser; there is no server.

1. Where the Sun and the Earth are. Their positions relative to the Moon come from the open-source Astronomy Engine, with the IAU model of the Moon's rotation. They are computed exactly every two hours and interpolated in between, so that every mission is sampled every ten minutes.

2. What the terrain hides. From the site, rays are marched over NASA's LOLA elevation model in every direction, every 0.25°, out to 400 km on the curved Moon. The highest elevation angle found along each ray is the skyline. The 120 m model is used for the marked sites and around any point clicked on the map.

3. What the Earth hides. The Earth's disc, enlarged by 75 km of opaque air as in NASA's eclipse predictions, is tested against the Sun's.

4. What it means. The Sun counts as up when the chosen fraction of its disc is above the skyline and not covered by the Earth; the Earth when it clears the skyline by the chosen margin. From the samples come the shares of time, the windows, the longest night and the longest link gap.

5. The whole map at once. The terrain is resampled along the direction of the light, and one running maximum per row tells all 1.26 million places south of 80° S at once whether they see it. One moment takes about a tenth of a second, so the map is computed live, in background workers.

HOW FAR IT CAN BE TRUSTED

Sun and Earth directions against NASA/JPL Horizons, 9,810 reference values: largest difference 0.004° (the Sun's disc is 0.53° wide).

Earth elevation at two real landings against a JPL report: IM-1, 15.4° on the landing day (JPL: 15°); Chandrayaan-3, 13.0° above the horizontal (JPL: about 11° above the local terrain).

Share of time with sunlight and with the Earth in view against the NASA LOLA-team illumination maps, 400 places over 18.6 years: correlation 0.98 for both.

Eclipses against NASA's predictions for the 14 lunar eclipses of 2025-2030: 58 contact times within 8.3 s. The other two, of the eclipse that only grazes the Moon (18 July 2027), within 52 s.

The eclipse of 14 March 2025 at the Blue Ghost Mission 1 landing site against the mission's own prediction: first and last contact within half a minute.

317 automated tests. Every figure can be reproduced with a command given in the repository. The limits are stated there too: this is geometry (line of sight to the Sun and the Earth), not a power or radio-link budget; terrain is modelled south of 80° S; it is a planning aid, not a flight product.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Mission planners can shortlist sites and dates in seconds instead of assembling the answer from specialist tools, with numbers traceable to NASA sources and a link that lets a colleague see exactly the same comparison. When a schedule slips, the calendar shows at once what another landing day would give.

Educators can show why the south pole is hard: the Sun circling the horizon, a ridge hiding it for days, the Earth hanging low over one side of the sky.

Anyone curious can pick a place on the Moon and see what a lander would see.

WHAT IS CREATIVE, AND WHAT WE CONSIDERED

The tool does not print angles: it draws the skyline the lander would see and puts the Sun and the Earth against it, so that the answer is read at a glance, and it compares scenarios on one screen. The map is not a stored picture: it is computed live for 1.26 million places with a method made for the purpose, so it follows the date, the rules and the height of the panels. We considered what decides a polar mission and is easy to overlook: the real terrain rather than a smooth sphere, the height of the panels above the ground, grazing radio links, eclipses, and how far each number can be trusted, which is why every result is checked against NASA references and the limits are written next to the results.

Next: the north pole, and energy and radio-link budgets on top of the geometry.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

TypeScript; Preact for the interface; Vite for the build; Vitest for the tests; Astronomy Engine for the positions of the Sun and the Moon; Web Workers for the map; Python for the script that fetches the reference tables from NASA/JPL Horizons; GitHub Pages for hosting. Open source under the Apache License 2.0.

Live application: https://m4tt187.github.io/lunar-landing-site-navigator/

JPL IPN Progress Report 42-240: Earth elevations at the IM-1 and Chandrayaan-3 landings
NASA, Lunar Site Selection (Moon to Mars Architecture white paper, NTRS 20230016267)
projectRefs: Astronomy Engine 2.1.19 by Don Cross (MIT License): positions of the Sun and the Moon
